messages.subject: Re: R/qtl version 1.08-56
messages.body_plain:
Dear Karl,

I’m enjoying to play with 1.08-56. Its functions are very well
organized and easy to use!
By the way, I found the different result of scantwo between 1.07-12
and 1.08-56 using the same data set. Did you update scantwo as well
when you released 1.08-56?
I’m wondering because one of my main QTL-QTL interaction was
disappeared in the result of scantwo 1.08-56.
Unfortunately, I discarded version 1.07-12. If its possible, can I
have version 1.07-12? So I can recheck whether something wrong with my
data.

I love rqtl and hope rqtl will stay around for long-long time!
Thank you.

Best,
Masato

messages.subject: Re: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
I'm running twoscan on the Brem QTL dataset (using multiple
regression), and most of the high interaction lod scores are for
marker pairs which are very close together. (maybe one or two
recombinations in the whole dataset)

So my ouput looks like:
marker1   marker2
1              2
1              3
1              4
100            102
100           103
etc...

I know that such occurances should never happen, as the markers are so
close that they practically share the same phenotype data.

This might have something to do with the way I'm calculating the
interaction lod score. I would like to confirm that the way I
calculate the interaction score from the out$lod matrix is correct:

	#Compute output LOD scores
	pair = 1;
	for (m1 in 1:(num_markers-1))
	{
		for (m2 in (m1+1):num_markers)
		{
			scores[pair,1] = m1
			scores[pair,2] = m2
			scores[pair,3] = out$lod[m2,m1] - out$lod[m1,m2]   #The interaction
score (epistasis)

			pair = pair + 1;
		}
	}

Thanks for your help,
Greg

messages.subject: Re: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
Actually, I think the issue is with the regression itself. Neighboring
marker pairs have very few recombinations, so if those one or two of
those phenotype values are extreme, the pair gets a strong lod score
regardless of the statistical power.

Is there a way to report values only of a particular power? (possibly
report p-values rather than lod scores?) Can marker pairs with less
than let's say 5 recombinations be discarded? I could post-process the
results, but I'm afraid these extra scores have muddled the
permutation tests.

 - Greg

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
A simpler way to calculate the interaction LOD scores is to
use upper.tri or lower.tri, as follows:

   intlod <- (out$lod - t(out$lod))[lower.tri(out$lod)]

Regarding high interaction LOD scores for tightly linked positions,
I generally would ignore two points that aren't separated by a marker;
you can zero out such regions using the clean function.

   data(hyper)
   hyper <- calc.genoprob(subset(hyper, chr=1:4), step=2.5)
   out <- scantwo(hyper)

   plot(out)
   plot( clean(out) )

For the case of multiple markers with the same genotype data, I don't
have any useful advice.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
The p-values would be a monotonic transformation of the LOD scores,
so that wouldn't help.

You could write a function to zero out any particular regions of the
scantwo results, and you could use that in the permutation tests, but
all we've done is to include an option which zeros out points not
separated by a marker.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: R/qtl version 1.08-56
messages.body_plain:
Analysis with scantwo will consider only the phenotyped individuals.

If there is appreciable missing marker genotype data or the markers
are not very dense, you may need a larger number of imputations (n.draws
in sim.geno).  If you run sim.geno and then scantwo a second time and
get rather different results, you should probably increase the number of
imputations.

karl

messages.subject: Re: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
I'm happy to write a function to zero out regions with small
recombination rates, but I don't see how that can be incorporated into
permutation testing. The perm object only contains a few numbers
relating to each permutation, so the zeroing would have to be done
before running permutations. But, scantwo determines valid pairs from
the original genotype matrix, and that can't be modified to blank
individual pairs. Is there an intermediate step I missed? Can scantwo
accept a list of pairs to test rather than using all pairs?

On a somewhat different note, I would like to know how the results of
scantwo/perms is used to determine a LOD/alpha table. For a given lod
type (ie. interaction), there is only one lod score from each
permutation and a df value. What formula is used to convert the list/
df into alpha values?

I really appreciate all of your assistance,
Greg

messages.subject: Re: Permutation Testing
messages.body_plain:
I have a suggestion (more like a hack) about the high interaction LODs
for markers that are very close.  The essential problem, as has been
pointed out,  is that we have collinearity between markers that are
very close.  One way to get rid of collinearity is to use regularized
regression, where, instead of minimizing the sum of squares with
respect to the regression coefficients, you minimize rss(b) +
lambda*sum(b^2) or rss(b) + lambda*sum(abs(b)), where rss(b) is the
residual sum of squares, b are the regression coefficients and lambda
is a smoothing parameter.

This type of regularization will automatically downweight LOD scores
with low power (low information).

In principle, implementing this is not hard, but requires great care
because of the central and crucial role of the scanone function.

One can approximate this by augmenting your data with fake data, with,
say 1000 individuals and average phenotypes.  Then analyze your data
giving the fake observations low weight using the "weight" option in
scanone.  When you permute, make sure you use stratified permutations
(keep the fake data in one stratum).

Saunak
